newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers' strike - breakdown of sectors.
newsitem.headline: French truckers' strike - breakdown of sectors.

text.p: A nine-day-old French truckers' strike has taken a heavy toll on France's fuel and farm industries and threatens hundreds of businesses and factories cut off from markets and suppliers, industry officials said on Tuesday.

Refineries and fuel depots were among the primary targets of the truckers, who have erected nearly 180 roadblocks to push for higher wages, shorter working hours and earlier retirement. On Monday they started to close in on the capital.
Truckers' unions and employers said they made little progress in a fifth round of talks on Tuesday.
Fuel shortages and rationing were reported in many regions, coastal fishermen pulled up their lines as perishable goods rotted on clogged roads, and many food stores ran low on fresh produce.
The following is a breakdown of affected sectors.
PETROL/FUEL - Truckers on Tuesday sealed off a petrol depot at Grigny which supplies 90 percent of petrol sold in hypermarkets in the Paris region.
The Oil Industry Association said half the nation's 175 fuel depots were blocked. Heating fuel was getting through, but 500 out of 18,000 petrol stations were dry, up from 100 on Monday.
Shell's largest French refinery, in Rouen, a Total refinery at Notre-Dame-de-Gravenchon, and the Grandpuits refinery in Seine-et-Marne were sealed off by truckers.
In Normandy, all petrol depots and refineries near Rouen were cut off. In certain regions including the Pas-de-Calais, officials are rationing petrol supplies to private car owners.
Local authorities in many areas ordered petrol stations to supply only firemen, ambulances and other emergency services, or ration sales to private motorists.
GRAIN - The strike has begun to disrupt grain supplies to French ports, silo officials said on Tuesday.
"Most access roads are blocked, but the main concern is petrol shortages," one official said.
In the northern port of Dunkirk, silo officials said trucks could still use the Paris-Lille highway to supply silos.
Another official said inventories were low, and that if the strike lasted one more week, ship loadings could be disrupted.

In the southwestern port of Bordeaux officials at the SIGMA silo said the strike was curtailing grain supplies activity. But because silos are full of newly harvested maize, ship loadings are proceeding at the normal pace, he said.
AGRO-FOOD - The sector is temporarily shedding workers and could run up big losses if the strike goes on, industry officials said on Tuesday.
"If the situation were to last two or three more days, we could all be on temporary leave," said Philippe Cousseau, head of logistics for the National Agro-Food Industry Association.
He said producers of dairy products, poultry, ready-made meals, fruits and vegetables were among the hardest hit by the crisis, which could result in "very heavy" financial losses.
The fruits and vegetables industry association, Interfel, said shipping had slowed to a crawl because of fuel shortages.
Fruits and vegetable sales were down 10 to 50 percent across the nation. Sales at the Rungis wholesale food market near Paris were down 30 percent, said Interfel director Remy Leprette.
Animal feed producers, whose inventories are low, are running short of sunflower and rapemeals.

Around 20 animal feed plants have temporary laid off staff and 100 more, out of a total of 380, may be affected by Wednesday, said Paul Hervieu, spokesman of the National Animal Feed Makers Association. He warned that if the strike went on longer, farmers would have trouble feeding pigs and chickens.
A spokeswoman for Danone, a major producer of dairy products, said, "We are doing all we can to supply retailers. If the situation were to last, we would be worried."
Many small fresh food businesses unable to make deliveries, such as Nutrition et Sante in Revel in the Haute Garonne, halted production after cramming their storage spaces.
RETAIL - Supermarkets in the lorry-besieged towns of Caen, Bordeaux and Avignon were the hardest hit by the strike.
"We got the feeling this morning that the strike movement is getting tougher, particularly in the North where the Vendin warehouse is cut off," said a Promodes spokesman.
"Three of our trucks are blocked in Normandy, resulting in 500,000 francs in lost merchandise right there," he said.
Retailers gave no estimate of the strike's total cost.
Carrefour, which has a policy of encouraging local supplies for its superstores, appears less affected.

"Right now, we don't have too many problems other than fuel shortages in the Bordeaux region, Cote d'Azur, Nice and Antibes," a Carrefour spokesman said. "This week, we're all right, but beyond that, we risk having problems."
Privately-owned hypermarkets group Auchan said the situation varied greatly from region to region.

CARGO - Air France Cargo said the situation would become critical if the strike continued. "The situation has become difficult, with services running behind schedule. However, we have not yet reached crisis point which could be the case if the dispute were prolonged," an airline official said.
The airline's trucking services are hardest hit around Bordeaux, the Spanish and German borders, and the port towns of Calais and Dover, the official said.
Air France trucks left from Paris/Charles de Gaulle (CDG) as scheduled for destinations in France and Europe after lorry drivers lifted a barricade near the airport on Monday evening.
A CDG-based forwarder cancelled its twice-daily trucking shuttle service between Paris and Lyon on Tuesday.

"Roads in most regions are affected, particularly in eastern France, where we have vehicles stuck in traffic en route to Frankfurt. Some in-bound freight to CDG this evening just won't arrive in time to make flight connections," he said.

CARS - The truckers' strike has disrupted production at several car plants unable to obtain parts but the impact is muted because production slowdowns had been scheduled as a result of weak demand for cars.
Renault has set short-time working for 24 hours at its Sandouville plant, which produces Safrane and Laguna models, beginning on Tuesday afternoon.

Production at its Douai plant, which produces the new Megane Scenic, was halted this morning and may not resume until the strike ends, a spokeswoman said. All the access roads to the plant are sealed off.
Renault's Flins plant is expected to run out of supplies this afternoon. Flins produces components for Renault's installation in Slovenia which may be affected on Wednesday.

The PSA group's Peugeot and Citroen divisions said their plants were all running until tomorrow, but they could not guarantee what would happen beyond then. "Our visibility is very limited," a Peugeot spokesman said.
The Peugeot car division last week set short-time working at its Sochaux and Poissy plants in France, at its Madrid plant and its Ryton plant in Britain.
A Citroen spokesman said short-time working set for Friday at the Rennes plant had been brought forward to Monday.
